title: Query complexity of conditional equivalence testing
formal: Determine, up to multiplicative constant factors, the dependence on domain size \(n\) of the randomized adaptive conditional-query complexity \(Q(n,\varepsilon)\) of testing equality of two unknown distributions, for every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/4]\). The task is to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\ge\varepsilon\) with error at most \(1/3\), using the model below. The answer must give a positive comparison function \(F(n,\varepsilon)\), a uniform tester attaining its upper bound, and for every fixed permitted \(\varepsilon\) constants \(c_{\varepsilon},C_{\varepsilon}>0\) and \(n_0(\varepsilon)\) such that \[c_{\varepsilon}F(n,\varepsilon)\le Q(n,\varepsilon)\le C_{\varepsilon}F(n,\varepsilon)\qquad(n\ge n_0(\varepsilon)).\] Multiplicative factors depending on \(n\), including iterated logarithms, must be resolved rather than suppressed.
why: Conditional sampling exposes relative probabilities inside chosen parts of a domain and can dramatically reduce the amount of data needed for comparison. The remaining dependence on domain size measures the cost of comparing two wholly unknown laws even with this strong access. The central gap is now closed up to iterated-logarithmic factors; the exact growth requested by the source still requires distinguishing those factors.
status_note: The main gap posed in 2017 was resolved at the soft-asymptotic scale by the published SODA 2024 lower bound. The source’s exact-dependence request is interpreted here as constant-factor matching, which is not established by the checked upper and lower bounds because they retain iterated-logarithmic factors. On 15 September 2026, the source page, original model, upper bound, 2024 theorem/proof scale and distinct 2026 interactive setting were checked. A bounded later-work search did not verify a full constant-factor resolution; the status is uncertain rather than an unqualified claim that the old gap remains open. Complete proofs were not independently verified in Lean.

progress.text: Falahatgar and coauthors obtain \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-5}\log\log n)\) queries in their closeness-testing formulation. For fixed proximity this is double-logarithmic up to further logarithmic factors, not an established ordinary \(O(\log\log n)\) bound.

Acharya–Canonne–Kamath establish an \(\Omega(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) lower bound for adaptive equivalence testing, proving that domain-independent conditional identity testing does not extend to two unknown distributions.
Problem 87 asks for the exact dependence on domain size at constant proximity, continuing the earlier question about the gap between the known upper and lower bounds.

Chakraborty–Chakraborty–Kumar prove \(\widetilde\Omega(\log\log n)\) queries are necessary. Their Theorem 1.1 explicitly hides factors polynomial in \(\log\log\log n\), and Section 4.3 works at the scale \(\log\log n/\log\log\log n\). The construction uses total variation distance \(1/4\); it is also a valid lower-bound instance for each smaller fixed proximity. This closes the main gap while leaving the constant-factor target unestablished by these bounds.

The ITCS work on interactive proofs adds a data-rich prover and conditional comparison queries. It does not give the matching unassisted equivalence-testing bound required here. A bounded later-work search was completed on 15 September 2026.

sentences: Two unknown distributions must be distinguished as equal or separated by a fixed positive total variation distance.
Each conditional query selects one distribution and a nonempty subset, then receives a fresh sample restricted to that subset.
The target is matching constant-factor query bounds as the domain grows, allowing arbitrary adaptive queries and constants depending on the fixed proximity.
The main gap was closed in 2024 up to iterated-logarithmic factors, which are not hidden by this card’s answer criterion.
The result would pin down the remaining domain-size cost of comparing two unknown distributions under powerful conditional access.

definitions: A distribution on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), for an integer \(n\ge2\), is a function \(p:[n]\to[0,1]\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p(i)=1\); probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers and may vanish. Neither input distribution is explicitly known. Their total variation distance is \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}|p(i)-q(i)|.\] The tester receives \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers. A query specifies one of the two oracles and a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), represented by its full \(n\)-bit membership vector. For oracle \(p\), write \(p(S)=\sum_{i\in S}p(i)\). If \(p(S)>0\), the response is an element \(i\in S\) with probability \(p(i)/p(S)\). If \(p(S)=0\), the response is a uniformly random element of \(S\), with no failure flag. The same rule applies to \(q\). Each call uses fresh randomness conditional on its selected oracle and set; no probability value or set mass is revealed. Drawing from both distributions counts as two queries. Unconditional sampling is allowed by taking \(S=[n]\). All nonempty subsets are allowed, and later queries may depend on every previous response and internal random choice. The tester is a finite probabilistic Turing oracle program using independent fair random bits and no advice or other oracle. It must terminate on every execution; its local computation, subset-description length and storage have no imposed bound. Query cost is the worst-case total number of calls to both oracles, over input distributions, internal randomness and oracle responses. A correct tester accepts with probability at least \(2/3\) whenever \(p=q\), and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) whenever \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\ge\varepsilon\); either answer is allowed at intermediate positive distance. Probabilities include both sources of randomness. Let \(Q(n,\varepsilon)\) be the least worst-case query bound at these parameters among uniform testers correct on every permitted parameter pair and every input pair. Such finite bounds exist, for example from ordinary finite-domain distribution testing. The target studies \(n\to\infty\) separately at each fixed \(\varepsilon\); constants and the starting order may depend on \(\varepsilon\). It does not ask for optimal joint dependence when \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero with \(n\).
answer_criterion: Provide the matching bounds and uniform upper-bound tester specified in the formal statement, with complete Lean-checked correctness and complexity proofs. The lower bound must apply to every randomized adaptive tester in the stated conditional model. Bounds differing by unbounded functions of \(n\), even powers of \(\log\log\log n\), do not meet the constant-factor precision. A restatement of the defining optimum, fixed-size experiments, or results requiring a known reference distribution, a prover, probability evaluation or restricted conditioning sets are insufficient.

context_blocks.text: In identity testing one of the two distributions is supplied explicitly. In equivalence testing both distributions are hidden behind sampling oracles. This information difference remains significant even when samples can be conditioned on arbitrary subsets: a comparison against a known reference and a comparison between two unknown sources need not have the same sample cost.

A conditional query requests a fresh draw from the original probability law restricted to a chosen set. It does not return the probability of reaching that set. The rule for zero-mass sets matters because the tester does not know either support in advance. This card adopts the uniform-response convention stated explicitly in the 2024 lower-bound paper.

The source fixes a positive proximity parameter and asks how complexity grows with the domain. Accordingly, this card permits constants depending on that fixed parameter, while requiring matching dependence on domain size. The worst-case query convention includes both oracles and permits unrestricted adaptivity; it is not an expected query budget or a limit on the number of adaptive rounds.

The 2015 upper bound and 2024 lower bound both have double-logarithmic main terms, with additional iterated-logarithmic factors hidden by soft asymptotic notation. The later paper explicitly describes its result as resolving the earlier gap. That is a major resolution at the soft-asymptotic scale, but it does not establish matching constant factors. This card records that progress rather than carrying forward the obsolete square-root gap from the 2017 problem page.

The COLT source uses unnormalized \(\ell_1\) distance, twice total variation, and a different constant error probability. Those constant changes do not change the fixed-proximity asymptotic question. By contrast, suppressing a factor that grows with the domain would change the requested precision, so the problem page's displayed upper bound is recorded here with its missing soft-asymptotic qualification restored.

source_formulation.text: For constant positive proximity, determine the exact dependence of conditional equivalence-testing sample complexity on the domain size.
source_formulation.scope_note: Constant-factor asymptotic precision makes the source’s exact-dependence wording explicit. The interval of fixed proximity values is (0,1/4], covering the lower-bound regime; no claim of a uniform two-parameter optimum is made. The 2024 soft-asymptotic resolution is retained prominently.
